### If we're hurting, look outward
If this is what the shock looks like in a country that produces enormous amounts of its own oil, grows enormous amounts of its own food and borrows in its own currency, consider what it looks like where the buffers were never deep to begin with.
The imbalance is stark.
Food accounts for about **43% of household consumption in low-income developing countries** , according to the IMF, compared with just **12% in advanced economies**. (And given [the recent cuts to SNAP](https://substack.com/redirect/c0917b37-7ef6-4178-9ceb-99dafdcc0694?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), America contains _both_ advanced and poor economies, in my reading.)
So the same increase in the price of food does not mean the same thing.
For one household, it may mean a larger grocery bill and less discretionary spending.
For another, **there is no discretionary spending left to cut.
**
Import-dependent countries face another mechanism Americans rarely have to think about: **foreign exchange**.
Oil is traded internationally in hard currencies, overwhelmingly dollars. When the world price of fuel rises, an importing country has to send more scarce foreign currency abroad merely to buy the same physical quantity of energy.
That gives its government a miserable set of choices.
It can subsidize fuel and bleed public money and foreign-exchange reserves.
It can let domestic prices rise and hit households and businesses directly.
It can reduce imports and produce shortages.
Or, most commonly, it can do some combination of all three.
Higher fuel costs then raise the price of transportation, fertilizer, food production and industrial output. Higher imports worsen the country's trade balance. Foreign-exchange reserves fall. A weaker currency makes the next shipment of oil or wheat even more expensive.
**That is how a tanker problem thousands of miles away can become a dinner-table problem in a country nowhere near the war.**
The IMF, World Bank and World Food Programme warned in April that the burden would fall most heavily on low-income, import-dependent economies already carrying high debt and limited fiscal space.
By June, it was no longer a warning.
WFP examined three very different countries:
* SOMALIA imports **100% of its oil and 90% of its cereals**. WFP estimates that an additional 2.5 million people risk becoming unable to afford a basic food basket this year. The share of Somali households unable to meet their essential needs could rise from 47% last year (already a deep crisis) to almost 60% this year--from fewer than half of households to roughly **three in five**.
* SRI LANKA gets 63% of its energy from the Middle East. 44% of its remittances -- a critical source of economic income and national resilience -- come from Sri Lankans working abroad in the Middle East, while 45% of its tea exports go there. War disrupts both the remittance income from laborers sending money home, _and_ the export income, from selling its tea abroad. WFP says up to 1.3 million additional people there may be unable to meet their basic food needs, on top of an existing baseline of 4.7 million. That is potentially an increase of roughly **28%**.
* AFGHANISTAN already had 13.8 million people facing food insecurity before the crisis. If the Pakistan border remains closed and the Middle East crisis escalates, WFP estimates up to another 2.3 million could join them--an increase of as much as **17 percent on top of an already catastrophic baseline**.

And in many of these places, food is still sitting in the market. Families simply cannot afford it.
That is what a price shock looks like from the bottom: **full shelves and empty pockets.
**
The damage also does not neatly track along with the headlines.
Farmers plant and fertilize on biological calendars, not diplomatic ones. If fertilizer is unavailable or unaffordable during the week a crop needs it, delivering that fertilizer three months later does not rewind the growing season. The result appears -- _later --_ as a thinner harvest, reduced supply and higher prices.
And food systems use energy at nearly every stage: irrigation, fertilizer production, harvesting, food processing, refrigeration and transportation. WFP reports that the basic cost of a diet in Sudan has risen almost **40% since February** , driven in part by higher fuel prices.
The humanitarian response itself is being hit by exactly the same mechanics. WFP is paying about **20% more for ocean shipping and 35% more for aviation fuel**.
So the same crisis does two things at once: _it creates more people who need help, and makes every aid dollar reach fewer of them._
Meanwhile, humanitarian funding has been collapsing. In Somalia, which was already living through conflict and repeated drought, WFP helped hold off famine in 2022 by reaching millions of people. Today its reach is dramatically smaller even as exposure to food-price shocks is widening. Afghanistan's humanitarian system faces similar funding constraints.
None of these economies had much spare resilience to spend before this shock arrived.

And then there is today's news.
On Monday, Bangladesh raised fuel prices again. Diesel jumped from 115 taka a liter to 135--a **17.4% increase overnight** , following previous hikes in April and June.
The state-owned Bangladesh Petroleum Corporation had accumulated roughly **$1.9 billion in losses -- in USD -- between March and August** by selling fuel domestically for less than it cost to import.
Spread across those six months, that is on the order of **$10 million USD a day** being absorbed just to cushion the shock.
Eventually, the inevitable arithmetic forced the choice back into public view.
_**Raise prices, spend reserves, borrow more, ration fuel:**_ there is no fourth option that makes the imported energy bill disappear.
Bangladesh's garment industry--the foundation of its export economy--is already struggling with energy shortages and thin margins. So a fuel shock becomes an industrial shock, an employment shock, _and_ a foreign-exchange shock... which can circle back and make the next fuel shipment harder to afford.
An energy shock arrives first as inflation. But that's only its first name. After inflation, comes shortage: of fertilizer, then transport, then food. Poor, import-dependent countries, and households spending almost half their money on food, face the deeper consequences first -- but the sequence is the same.

### The good news, and what it can't do
I know what a skeptical reader is thinking, because it's what I would be thinking.
Didn't the price of oil just fall?
It did.
On Monday this week, Brent crude fell to around $100 a barrel, its lowest level in nearly two weeks, while U.S. crude dropped below $100. Traders were responding to recovering Saudi exports and the possibility of renewed U.S.-Iran diplomacy.
Take the good news.
Markets respond quickly when additional barrels become available or when traders think future supply may improve. Adaptation is exactly what this essay has been describing.
But there is a critical distinction between **price** and**physical condition**.
A _futures market_ reprices tomorrow every minute.
A _storage tank_ refills **only when a physical barrel arrives.**
Oil prices can fall sharply because traders think several million additional barrels _might_ reach the market next month.
> That does not put back the 507 million barrels already drawn out of global inventories.
> It does not repair three Saudi pumping stations on a continent-supporting pipeline.
> It does not replenish emergency stocks governments released in March.
> It does not reopen a fertilizer window that closed on a farmer in May.
> And it does not make freight at more than $30 a barrel economically equivalent to the shipping system the war destroyed.
The futures price is important.
But it is not a fuel gauge.
The number that tells you whether this system can absorb another serious disruption is not simply Tuesday's closing price.
It is how much **physical redundancy** remains underneath it.

### Risk, not prophecy
I am not going to tell you the shelves will be empty by January.
Some commentators have put a date on it. I don't think the evidence supports a date, and an argument that stakes everything on one is easy to dismiss the moment it passes.
Prices can fall.
Diplomacy can work.
Pipelines can be repaired.
China still has substantial inventory.
Demand can... _adjust ..._ further.
What the evidence supports is narrower, and to me more unsettling.
**We have learned that the global energy system can absorb an astonishing shock.**
_We have not learned that it can absorb the**same shock indefinitely** after drawing down the inventories, spare routes, suppressed demand and cheap logistics that carried it through the first six months._
Here's the sequence we've been through so far:
* **Flow is disrupted.**
* Stored inventory fills part of the gap.
* Alternative routes substitute for lost flow.
* Those routes become constrained.
* Prices suppress demand.
* Suppressed demand itself becomes another buffer.
* The world's largest suppressed buyer begins returning.

And as each buffer becomes thinner or more expensive, more of the adjustment has to happen through price--or through people simply consuming less.
On September 16, energy executives at Shell and Equinor warned that the market's "shock absorbers" were weakening. The IEA says essentially the same thing in numbers: rapidly falling inventories, damaged bypass routes and a global market increasingly dependent on expensive improvisation.
Follow this system all the way down and it stops being a story about tankers.
It runs from chokepoints to buffers, from buffers to prices, from prices to distribution, and from distribution to **people**.
It ends in whether a farmer can afford fertilizer, whether a trucking company can keep its rigs moving, whether a government has enough dollars left to buy another month's fuel--and whether a mother in Somalia, or Alabama, can afford cereal this month.
I don't think there is a border between the strategic question and the moral one.
It is the same system, followed to its end.

The question is no longer whether the system has shock absorbers.
We watched them work.
The question is how many more miles we expect to drive as they wear through.

Here is what has been spent, what is failing, and who is paying. | | ---|---|--- | | | Forwarded this email? ? for more ? Six months into the largest energy disruption in modern history, the world has coped by using up the things that made coping possible. Here is what has been spent, what is failing, and who is paying. | | | Sep 22 | | | | | | | | | | | | Where was the catastrophe? For six months a question has hung over this crisis: yes, fuel is up, life is tighter, but... where is the catastrophe? Before the war, the Strait of Hormuz was the conduit for roughly a fifth of the world's oil. In August, flows through it averaged just 7.6 million barrels a day, according to the International Energy Agency. Before the war, over 20 million barrels crossed the Strait per day--a drop of roughly 63%. Put differently, nearly two out of every three barrels that normally crossed Hormuz are no longer crossing it. Cumulative export losses through the strait are approaching 2.8 billion barrels. Back in April, the heads of the IMF, World Bank and World Food Programme said the war had already triggered one of the largest disruptions to global energy markets in modern history. And yet, the gas lines of the 1970s never came. The lights stayed on, the shelves stayed full, the gas stations stayed available (though expensive), and the trucks kept moving. Plenty of smart people have looked at that and concluded the system must be tougher than the pessimists believed. The observation is right. But the conclusion skips the question that matters most: what did the global energy system use to absorb the blow, and how much of it is left? | | ---|---|--- Savings are not income Picture a household that loses a paycheck. It gets by on savings, and if you only watched what was on the table for dinner, you might not notice anything had changed. That doesn't mean that paychecks stopped mattering. A hospital that loses grid power runs on generators, and the patients on ventilators keep breathing. That doesn't mean the electrical grid is irrelevant. The world has kept global supply chains functioning in large party by spending down savings. The US has drawn down our Strategic Petroleum Reserve to historic lows, and we're not alone. Reasonable people should be paying attention to how long that can continue. There is another useful distinction here, one of my favorite concepts in systems analysis: stocks versusflows. A stock is an inventory. A flow is movement between inventories. A reservoir -- a "stock" -- can keep water coming out of the faucet for awhile after the river feeding it weakens. (Both the faucet and the river are "flows.") If you watch only the faucet, everything looks fine. If you watch the reservoir falling, you understand how long "fine" can last. Oil production and imports are flows. Inventories are stocks. For six months, falling stocks have helped conceal a badly damaged flow. I have spent about twenty years working in sustainable farming, community land trusts, ecological infrastructure, and cooperative governance across five continents. The first thing that work teaches you is that a system 's health is measured by what it is standing on, not merely by whether it is running today. Here is what the world has been standing on since February. It started with luck. Oil markets entered this crisis in surplus. By the second half of last year, supply was running more than two million barrels a day ahead of demand, and the excess was filling storage tanks, most of all in China. Nobody planned that cushion for this war. It was simply there when the war arrived. Then came deliberate measures. IEA member countries released more than 300 million barrels from emergency reserves. Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates shoved as much crude as they could through pipelines and ports that bypass Hormuz, offsetting more than 500 million barrels of the loss. Producers outside the Gulf pumped harder. And the world simply used less. Economists call that last part demand destruction. It is a tidy phrase for factories slowing, trips not taken, businesses cutting production, governments rationing fuel, and people who simply cannot afford what they used to buy. The bypass story alone shows how hard the system adapted. Exports from Saudi Arabia's Yanbu terminal and the UAE's Fujairah port climbed from 4.1 million barrels a day in February to 7.8 million in June--a 90% increase in four months. The backup routes nearly doubled their workload. Then Houthi attacks and other Red Sea disruptions knocked that flow back to 5.5 million barrels a day by August--a loss of nearly 30 percent from the June peak -- before the Saudi East-West Pipeline itself was hit on September 10th. Even after all of that adaptation, the world has been pulling oil out of storage at a record 2.8 million barrels a day. Observed inventories now stand 507 million barrels below where they were when the war began. August alone drew down another 95 million barrels--almost one-fifth of the entire six-month inventory loss in a single month--showing that the rate of drawdown is still increasing. That's disconcerting, to say the least. The IEA's September 18 commentary contains a sentence everyone should read twice: "if Gulf supplies stay constrained while commercial stocks keep falling, higher prices and further cuts in demand may be needed to balance the market. " Translated out of economist: if more supply cannot get through, and there is less stored oil available to cover the gap, the thing that eventually has to give is consumption. Prices will rise until enough people, businesses and countries stop buying. So the honest description of the last six months is not that the shock was avoided. The shock was financed. We paid for it out of stored oil, emergency reserves, spare infrastructure, increased production elsewhere, and consumption people could no longer afford. You cannot finance the same structural deficit out of savings forever. The way around the chokepoint got hit The savings weren't the only thing holding. The routes that let oil pass around Hormuz were, too. They are now under fire. On September 10 and 11, drones struck Saudi Arabia's East-West Pipeline, the 1,200-kilometer line that carries crude across the kingdom to Yanbu on the Red Sea, where tankers can load without going near Hormuz. Reuters reported that three pumping stations were damaged. Industry sources estimated five to six weeks for full repairs, with partial pumping potentially returning sooner. The pipeline had been carrying roughly 4 to 5 million barrels a day. That is 4 to 5% of the world 's oil supply -- roughly one barrel out of every 20 to 25 produced on Earth -- moving through one piece of infrastructure across Saudi Arabia. As of Monday, no crude loadings had been observed at Yanbu since September 16. Aramco has also halted or postponed some deliveries to European refiners, including contracted October supplies that should have been absolute baseline supply for Europe's energy systems. Here is the part that would be funny if it weren't so expensive. With the bypass around Hormuz damaged, Saudi Arabia has pushed more of its crude back out through Hormuz --the very chokepoint the bypass was built to avoid. Saudi exports sank to about 2.4 million barrels a day in August, their lowest since at least 2013, and have rebounded above 4 million so far in September. Saudi crude is increasingly being carried out of the Persian Gulf and transferred to other tankers anchored off Oman--a ship-to-ship relay system that was unusual at anything like this scale before the war. Those ship-to-ship transfers are now moving roughly 2.5 million barrels a day, up from 1.4 million in August: an increase of almost 80% in one month. And moving the same barrel this way costs a lot, and consumes dramatically more infrastructure. A normal supply chain is designed so a tanker loads, sails, unloads and goes somewhere else. In a shuttle system, ships spend more time repositioning, waiting, transferring cargo and making additional legs. Kpler estimates that moving 3 million barrels a day through these workarounds could require 36 to 40 additional VLCC (very large carrying capacity) supertankers under its base case. Where do those ships come from? And if they're doing this, what else are they not doing? (If transfers have to move farther away to Malaysia, the requirement could rise as high as 58.) This is an important distinction in systems resilience: a workaround can preserve capacity while destroying efficiency. The oil may still arrive, but every barrel requires more ships, more crews, more insurance, more fuel, more time and more functioning pieces of infrastructure to get there. That expense is showing up immediately. Freight on a supertanker carrying Gulf crude to China has climbed above $30 per barrel , by far the highest on record. A barrel holds 42 gallons. That means the tanker trip alone can now add the equivalent of roughly 71 cents per gallon of crude before the oil has been refined, piped inland, trucked anywhere, taxed or sold at a filling station. A bypass does not make a chokepoint irrelevant... if destroying the bypass forces you back through the chokepoint. I want to be careful describing Hormuz itself, because "closed" is the loose version and it is easy to knock down. The strait is a severely constricted, militarized passage functioning through improvised exceptions, some of them backed by the U.S. military. Visible traffic is a trickle. Kpler counted 17 commodity vessels crossing over the latest weekend, down from 37 the weekend before, while some Gulf tankers are believed to be moving with their transponders off. That is not normal commerce. It is not zero either. The southern end of the Red Sea is in similar shape. Fifty-one vessels crossed the Bab el-Mandeb over the weekend, down from 57 the weekend before, so ships are still getting through. But Houthi attacks and related insecurity in the Red Sea had already helped cut exports from the Yanbu and Fujairah bypass ports from 7.8 million barrels a day in June to 5.5 million in August--a 29% retreat from the system 's emergency peak--before the Saudi pipeline itself was damaged. Call it what it is: two chokepoints that can no longer be counted on as ordinary commercial infrastructure. Nor should anyone build a plan around a quick diplomatic fix. Iranian officials have publicly attached substantial political and security conditions to fully restoring navigation -- including but not limited to, the removal of both Trump and Netanyahu from executive power -- while American and Iranian officials have also signaled varying degrees of openness to renewed diplomacy. Diplomacy may move quickly. It may not. It hasn't been a reliable avenue for solving this problem so far. A resilience plan that only works if diplomacy succeeds immediately is not much of a resilience plan. China: the shock absorber nobody voted for One of the biggest shock absorbers of the last six months got almost no attention. China bought halfthe oil they usually do. Think of the physical oil market as an auction with a finite number of cargoes available today. China is normally the biggest bidder in the room. If the biggest bidder suddenly stops bidding on millions of barrels every day, everybody else gets breathing room to secure their own supply--even though no new oil was produced. That is essentially what happened. According to the IEA, Chinese seaborne crude imports fell from about 11.5 million barrels a day in February to near 6 million in June. China nearly halved its seaborne crude buying --a drop of about 48%. China could afford to reduce purchases because it entered the crisis with enormous stored inventories, built partly during the cheaper oil environment of 2025. Beijing also nearly shut down fuel exports in early March. It wasn't acting out of generosity. It was protecting its own economy. But for everyone else, the systemic effect was the same as a gift: millions of barrels a day that the world 's largest importer would ordinarily have been competing to buy were suddenly left on the table. That is now changing. Chinese customs data show total crude imports recovering from roughly 7.1 million barrels a day in June to 8.93 million in August--about a 26% rebound in two months --while still remaining 23% below a year earlier. Its refineries processed 13.9 million barrels a day in August, up 11.2% from July and the highest rate since March. Beijing has eased fuel-export restrictions, allowing diesel and jet fuel to move back onto world markets. The loose version of this story says China's reserves are gone. They aren't. China is still drawing substantial volumes from storage. Reuters estimated a draw of about 639,000 barrels a day in August, the second-largest monthly draw of the war. What is changing is how the cushion is being used. China is running refineries harder, exporting fuel again and returning more actively to the crude market. That is the number to pay attention to: The global market is this tight while China is still importing roughly a quarter less crude than it did a year ago. If Chinese purchasing continues toward normal levels, it does not create additional oil. It simply puts the largest bidder back into the auction for the same constrained pool of available cargoes. The barrels China stops leaving on the table have to come from somewhere. From barrels to groceries Crude is the number on the news. Diesel is the number that reaches your groceries. To understand why, it helps to know what a refinery actually does. A refinery is not a big tank where crude goes in and whatever fuel society needs comes out. It is closer to an enormous, highly specialized industrial recipe. Different hydrocarbons boil, crack and react at different temperatures. The refinery's towers, catalytic crackers, hydrotreaters and other equipment are built to turn particular ranges of crude into particular mixtures of products. An average 42-gallon barrel processed by a U.S. refinery yields roughly 19 to 20 gallons of gasoline, 11 to 13 gallons of distillate fuel such as diesel and heating oil, and 3 to 5 gallons of jet fuel , plus a range of petrochemical feedstocks and other products. Refiners can shift that mix somewhat--but only within limits determined by the machinery they have and the chemistry of the crude going into it. That's important because diesel and jet fuel are both middle distillates. A refinery can shift their production mix somewhat toward one or the other, but it cannot simply turn every spare barrel of gasoline into diesel because diesel happens to be scarce this month. And not every crude oil is interchangeable. A refinery designed around particular grades of oil cannot necessarily substitute a radically different barrel without losing efficiency or changing equipment. So "there is enough crude somewhere in the world" is not the same thing as "there is enough diesel where it is needed." The physical chain looks more like this: Oil field -> tanker or pipeline -> refinery -> gasoline/diesel/jet fuel -> product storage -> pipeline/ship/truck -> local distributor -> end user. A bottleneck anywhere in that chain can create scarcity downstream even while the stage before it looks healthy. You can have crude and not enough refinery capacity. You can have refinery capacity and the wrong crude. You can have diesel sitting at a coastal terminal and not enough functioning inland transport to put it into farm machinery three states away. According to the IEA's September report, U.S. diesel prices passed the equivalent of $200 a barrel in early September, about 94% above pre-war levels. Almost doubling in eight months. Gulf refiners exported only about a quarter as much diesel in August as before the war, while Russian refined-product exports have been hammered by attacks on refinery infrastructure and export restrictions. Together, the Gulf and Russia are shipping roughly 1.6 million fewer barrels of diesel and gasoil every day than they did in February. Before the war, those two sources supplied almost 45% of the world's seaborne diesel trade. Refineries elsewhere are now being pushed hard to make up the difference. And this is where the price of oil becomes the price of dinner. Follow one loaf of bread backward. Diesel runs machinery on the farm. Energy is embedded in fertilizer. Trucks bring seed, fertilizer and other inputs to the farm. Diesel powers harvest machinery. Another truck moves grain to an elevator. More transportation brings it to a mill. Processing consumes energy. Another truck moves flour or finished bread to a warehouse or distribution center. Another truck unloads at the grocery store. The price of diesel does not touch a loaf of bread once. It can touch the fertilizer, the tractor, the grain truck, the miller 's deliveries, the warehouse andthe final truck to the supermarket. One energy shock can enter the cost of the same physical product at several different links in its journey. And there is a time lag. A trucking company pays more for fuel today. A wholesaler sees higher freight bills next month. Contracts reset for next quarter. Farmers decide what they can afford to plant at planting time (and cannot make up the difference later). Processors alter prices. Retailers eventually pass some portion on to you--potentially with price gouging added on top at any link in the chain. That is why the price shock at the pump can keep working its way into groceries months after the oil-market headline that started it has disappeared from the front page. If we're hurting, look outward If this is what the shock looks like in a country that produces enormous amounts of its own oil, grows enormous amounts of its own food and borrows in its own currency, consider what it looks like where the buffers were never deep to begin with. The imbalance is stark. Food accounts for about 43% of household consumption in low-income developing countries , according to the IMF, compared with just 12% in advanced economies. (And given , America contains both advanced and poor economies, in my reading.) So the same increase in the price of food does not mean the same thing. For one household, it may mean a larger grocery bill and less discretionary spending. For another, there is no discretionary spending left to cut. Import-dependent countries face another mechanism Americans rarely have to think about: foreign exchange. Oil is traded internationally in hard currencies, overwhelmingly dollars. When the world price of fuel rises, an importing country has to send more scarce foreign currency abroad merely to buy the same physical quantity of energy. That gives its government a miserable set of choices. It can subsidize fuel and bleed public money and foreign-exchange reserves. It can let domestic prices rise and hit households and businesses directly. It can reduce imports and produce shortages. Or, most commonly, it can do some combination of all three. Higher fuel costs then raise the price of transportation, fertilizer, food production and industrial output. Higher imports worsen the country's trade balance. Foreign-exchange reserves fall. A weaker currency makes the next shipment of oil or wheat even more expensive. That is how a tanker problem thousands of miles away can become a dinner-table problem in a country nowhere near the war. The IMF, World Bank and World Food Programme warned in April that the burden would fall most heavily on low-income, import-dependent economies already carrying high debt and limited fiscal space. By June, it was no longer a warning. WFP examined three very different countries: SOMALIA imports 100% of its oil and 90% of its cereals. WFP estimates that an additional 2.5 million people risk becoming unable to afford a basic food basket this year. The share of Somali households unable to meet their essential needs could rise from 47% last year (already a deep crisis) to almost 60% this year--from fewer than half of households to roughly three in five. SRI LANKA gets 63% of its energy from the Middle East. 44% of its remittances -- a critical source of economic income and national resilience -- come from Sri Lankans working abroad in the Middle East, while 45% of its tea exports go there. War disrupts both the remittance income from laborers sending money home, and the export income, from selling its tea abroad. WFP says up to 1.3 million additional people there may be unable to meet their basic food needs, on top of an existing baseline of 4.7 million. That is potentially an increase of roughly 28%. AFGHANISTAN already had 13.8 million people facing food insecurity before the crisis. If the Pakistan border remains closed and the Middle East crisis escalates, WFP estimates up to another 2.3 million could join them--an increase of as much as 17 percent on top of an already catastrophic baseline. And in many of these places, food is still sitting in the market. Families simply cannot afford it. That is what a price shock looks like from the bottom: full shelves and empty pockets. The damage also does not neatly track along with the headlines. Farmers plant and fertilize on biological calendars, not diplomatic ones. If fertilizer is unavailable or unaffordable during the week a crop needs it, delivering that fertilizer three months later does not rewind the growing season. The result appears -- later -- as a thinner harvest, reduced supply and higher prices. And food systems use energy at nearly every stage: irrigation, fertilizer production, harvesting, food processing, refrigeration and transportation. WFP reports that the basic cost of a diet in Sudan has risen almost 40% since February , driven in part by higher fuel prices. The humanitarian response itself is being hit by exactly the same mechanics. WFP is paying about 20% more for ocean shipping and 35% more for aviation fuel. So the same crisis does two things at once: it creates more people who need help, and makes every aid dollar reach fewer of them. Meanwhile, humanitarian funding has been collapsing. In Somalia, which was already living through conflict and repeated drought, WFP helped hold off famine in 2022 by reaching millions of people. Today its reach is dramatically smaller even as exposure to food-price shocks is widening. Afghanistan's humanitarian system faces similar funding constraints. None of these economies had much spare resilience to spend before this shock arrived. And then there is today's news. On Monday, Bangladesh raised fuel prices again. Diesel jumped from 115 taka a liter to 135--a 17.4% increase overnight , following previous hikes in April and June. The state-owned Bangladesh Petroleum Corporation had accumulated roughly $1.9 billion in losses -- in USD -- between March and August by selling fuel domestically for less than it cost to import. Spread across those six months, that is on the order of $10 million USD a day being absorbed just to cushion the shock. Eventually, the inevitable arithmetic forced the choice back into public view. Raise prices, spend reserves, borrow more, ration fuel: there is no fourth option that makes the imported energy bill disappear. Bangladesh's garment industry--the foundation of its export economy--is already struggling with energy shortages and thin margins. So a fuel shock becomes an industrial shock, an employment shock, and a foreign-exchange shock... which can circle back and make the next fuel shipment harder to afford. An energy shock arrives first as inflation. But that's only its first name. After inflation, comes shortage: of fertilizer, then transport, then food. Poor, import-dependent countries, and households spending almost half their money on food, face the deeper consequences first -- but the sequence is the same. The good news, and what it can't do I know what a skeptical reader is thinking, because it's what I would be thinking. Didn't the price of oil just fall? It did. On Monday this week, Brent crude fell to around $100 a barrel, its lowest level in nearly two weeks, while U.S. crude dropped below $100. Traders were responding to recovering Saudi exports and the possibility of renewed U.S.-Iran diplomacy. Take the good news. Markets respond quickly when additional barrels become available or when traders think future supply may improve. Adaptation is exactly what this essay has been describing. But there is a critical distinction between price andphysical condition. A futures market reprices tomorrow every minute. A storage tank refills only when a physical barrel arrives. Oil prices can fall sharply because traders think several million additional barrels might reach the market next month. That does not put back the 507 million barrels already drawn out of global inventories. It does not repair three Saudi pumping stations on a continent-supporting pipeline. It does not replenish emergency stocks governments released in March. It does not reopen a fertilizer window that closed on a farmer in May. And it does not make freight at more than $30 a barrel economically equivalent to the shipping system the war destroyed. The futures price is important. But it is not a fuel gauge. The number that tells you whether this system can absorb another serious disruption is not simply Tuesday's closing price. It is how much physical redundancy remains underneath it. Risk, not prophecy I am not going to tell you the shelves will be empty by January. Some commentators have put a date on it. I don't think the evidence supports a date, and an argument that stakes everything on one is easy to dismiss the moment it passes. Prices can fall. Diplomacy can work. Pipelines can be repaired. China still has substantial inventory. Demand can... adjust ... further. What the evidence supports is narrower, and to me more unsettling. We have learned that the global energy system can absorb an astonishing shock. We have not learned that it can absorb thesame shock indefinitely after drawing down the inventories, spare routes, suppressed demand and cheap logistics that carried it through the first six months. Here's the sequence we've been through so far: Flow is disrupted. Stored inventory fills part of the gap. Alternative routes substitute for lost flow. Those routes become constrained. Prices suppress demand. Suppressed demand itself becomes another buffer. The world's largest suppressed buyer begins returning. And as each buffer becomes thinner or more expensive, more of the adjustment has to happen through price--or through people simply consuming less. On September 16, energy executives at Shell and Equinor warned that the market's "shock absorbers" were weakening. The IEA says essentially the same thing in numbers: rapidly falling inventories, damaged bypass routes and a global market increasingly dependent on expensive improvisation. Follow this system all the way down and it stops being a story about tankers. It runs from chokepoints to buffers, from buffers to prices, from prices to distribution, and from distribution to people. It ends in whether a farmer can afford fertilizer, whether a trucking company can keep its rigs moving, whether a government has enough dollars left to buy another month's fuel--and whether a mother in Somalia, or Alabama, can afford cereal this month. I don't think there is a border between the strategic question and the moral one. It is the same system, followed to its end. The question is no longer whether the system has shock absorbers. We watched them work. The question is how many more miles we expect to drive as they wear through. BIBLIOGRAPHY: Sources Bosoni, Toril. Good Work Around Wyoming
| | | | | | [ ](https://ctrk.klclick.com/l/01M35E2HB97KHZM7PM314YCKY3_0)
---
| **Welcome to the Barlow for Wyoming Newsletter. Your hub for latest news, information and upcoming events.**
---
|
---
| | |
---
|
### **Good Work Around Wyoming**
---
| Hi friends,The more Kelly and I spend time in our Wyoming towns, the more we learn from the people we meet. This week, we saw businesses creating good jobs, programs helping families build self-sufficiency, and neighbors giving their time to serve others. We joined a celebration of culture and tradition and heard thoughtful questions from students about Wyoming’s future. There is much to be proud of around the Cowboy State.Everywhere we went, people took the time to welcome us and share what they’re working on. We're fortunate to have so much good happening across our state because people care enough to do the work.We heard from the Wyoming Supreme Court last week on education funding. Providing a great education for our students is a constitutional responsibility, and the opinion tells us where our funding model needs more work. The Legislature will have work to do in the upcoming session to make education funding whole. As governor, I’ll work to make sure Wyoming meets that responsibility.Early voting begins October 6. We’ll keep traveling and listening, and I hope you’ll make a plan to vote.Eric
---
| **In Case You Missed It...**
---
| **Barlow statement on State Supreme Court ruling related to education funding** “In Wyoming, providing a great education for our students is not only something we value, it is a constitutional responsibility. We want our students, teachers, and schools to have what they need to succeed. Today’s Supreme Court opinion lets us know exactly where our education funding model needs more work. The Legislature will have work to do to make education funding whole. As governor, I’ll work to make sure Wyoming meets that responsibility.”
---
| **VIDEO MESSAGING** We have most of the videos we have created posted on our Barlow for Wyoming Youtube page, which should make it easy for you to access and share them. You can access the page [here](https://ctrk.klclick.com/l/01M35E2HB97KHZM7PM314YCKY3_1)[

October 3, 9:00-11:00 am, Rock Springs Coffee with Eric and Kelly, Pin Up Coffee at the Train Depot, 501 S Main St., Rock Springs October 3, 12:30-3:00 pm, Watch Party: UW vs. North Dakota State Bison, Broadway Theater, 618 Broadway St., Rock Springs
---
| **On The Trail**
---
| | | | |
---
| | |
---
| | | | |
---
| **ETHETE** Kelly and I were honored to join students, families and community members for today’s Back to School Powwow at Wyoming Indian High School.I appreciated the opportunity to help carry the flag and take part in the Veterans Dance. I was honored to be recognized during the dance.Thank you to the Arapaho Warriors Legion Post 96 for the opportunity to participate, and to the Tribe and school for the warm welcome.It was great to see young people come together to celebrate culture, community and the start of a new school year!
---
|
---
| **LARAMIE** Kelly and I had a great time at Bonds Brewing Company in downtown Laramie!It was good to visit with folks, answer some questions and hear what’s on people’s minds.I always enjoy these opportunities to have a conversation, listen and catch up with people from the community.A special thanks to Jay and Mallory Bond for hosting this meet & greet. I appreciate everyone who came out and spent some time with us!
---
| | | | |
---
| | |
---
| | | | |
---
| | |
---
|
---
| | | **LARAMIE** It was great to spend some time with the Associated Students of the University of Wyoming (ASUW) and have meaningful conversations!We covered a lot of ground, including public lands, tribal sovereignty, public education, creative economies, and plenty more. I appreciate the thoughtful questions and willingness to talk about the issues that matter to Wyoming.I appreciated talking with Professor Dan Fetsco and Dr. Cecelia Aragon about their work at the University. I was especially honored to learn I was in Dan’s new book about my work in restoration of rights.Kelly also shared more about her initiative as First Lady, SITE — Service In The Everyday. She touched on the many ways we can all find opportunities to serve our communities.Thank you to everyone who joined us, asked questions, and shared their thoughts. Always nice to spend time with Wyoming students!
---
| | |
---
| | | | |
---
| | |
---
|
---
| **LARAMIE** Thank you to Brad Enzi with the Laramie Chamber Business Alliance for the great tour around Laramie! It’s always time well spent to see Wyoming’s good work.We visited Aurum Standards Group, HIVIZ Shooting Systems and RAVE Aerospace. From keeping skilled jobs in Laramie to manufacturing shooting accessories and developing technology for airlines, these businesses create opportunities to build careers right here in Wyoming.At Ivinson Memorial Hospital, Terry Moss coordinated our tour and discussion, giving us a firsthand look at the hospital’s work and the role it plays in serving the Laramie community. Ivinson Memorial Hospital works closely with the University, providing students in clinical studies with opportunities to gain hands-on experience at the hospital.We also stopped at the Downtown Clinic and Laramie Soup Kitchen, where staff, volunteers and local partners help neighbors get medical care, prescriptions and a good meal.I appreciate everyone who took time to visit and share their work with me. There’s a lot to be proud of in Laramie!
---
| | | | |
---
| | |
---
| | | | |
---
| | |
---
|
---
| | | | |
---
| **LARAMIE** Kelly and I were in Laramie to celebrate Climb Wyoming’s 40th anniversary. As a former board member, Kelly loved supporting the work that goes into helping single moms gain new skills, find good jobs and provide for their families.We heard from moms about how Climb changed their lives, and from a daughter who thanked her mother for completing the program so she could be there for her. That says everything about what this work means for the whole family.Thank you to the Climb team, employers and supporters who have made these opportunities possible for 40 years, and to the moms who stepped up and did the work.
---
| | | | |
---
| | |
---
|
---
| | | | |
---
| **GILLETTE** I attended the annual Memory of 8 run in Gillette last week. I was glad to emcee the event again this year as we remember the 8 University of Wyoming cross country runners lost in an accident 25 years ago, caused by a drunk driver. This event was created by the McLeland family, who lost Morgan McLeland in the accident.Members of the UW cross country team traveled to Gillette to join the event. It was good to meet them and see them carrying the memory of Cody, Kyle, Joshua, Justin, Morgan, Kevin, Nicholas and Shane forward
---
| | | | |
---
| | |
---
|
---
| | | **CASPER** Kelly and I were in Casper for the Boys & Girls Club 28th Annual Awards and Recognition Breakfast. Congratulations to Student of the Year, Brynn!Members of the community that have made a difference in the lives of young people were also recognized, including Bob and Celia Kirkwood, who focus much of their time giving back.Guest speaker Coach Ken Carter reminded us of the importance of education, mentorship, and support to our youth.Thank you to the Boys & Girls Club for what you do for Wyoming kids everyday.

# **AI Titans preached a pause then slashed prices 50%**
Amodei begged the industry to slow down. Tuesday he shipped anyway. Anthropic dropped Claude Opus 5.5 at about 40% cheaper to run than Opus 5. OpenAI answered with GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna and slashed API prices 50% versus GPT-5.6 promo rates. First releases since Coxon quit September 8 yelling they were "gambling with our lives."
* **Winners?** Customers drowning in AI bills and the Chinese open-weight shops. DeepSeek, Alibaba, and Moonshot forced a 40-50% cut without joining the extinction sermon.
* **Losers?** Amodei's pause-as-moat brand and every shop locked into last month's sticker. Altman and Musk joined the slowdown call. Then the labs cut the product anyway.
* **Next?** More cuts. Token efficiency becomes the only pitch that clears a procurement committee. Frontier labs keep preaching extinction while racing DeepSeek on price per task.

I called the **[pause-as-moat](https://substack.com/redirect/58f150d8-f694-46e3-85ef-b96c505967f4?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)**. They preached. Then they shipped. **[Same circus I named](https://substack.com/redirect/02054fbb-df38-4f70-8b61-59ee5d7dcaea?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg).** Coxon quit September 8. Tuesday they cut 40% and 50%. That's not a slowdown. That's a fire sale in a choir robe.

# **Robot Semi-Trucks just ran I-45 at $0.85 a mile**
Aurora stuffed CNBC in a driverless tractor trailer cab for three hours on I-45. Twenty trucks are live, 200 by year-end. They burned more than $800 million in 2025 and still aim at positive free cash flow in 2028. Bank of America prices it at about $0.85 a mile versus $1.30 for human wages. Morgan Stanley says 7.5 times the profit.
* **Winners?** Aurora if 20 becomes 200, and shippers buying miles at $0.85 instead of $1.30. Urmson sells hours the federal clock forbids a human to drive.
* **Losers?** Class 8 drivers on Hours-of-Service limits and skeptics like uShip's Sean Wu. Judgment and customer service don't show up on a per-mile invoice.
* **Next?** Watch the jump from 20 trucks to 200 by December. Miss that ramp and the 2028 free-cash-flow promise is just another fairy tale.

Three million miles since 2021. Fifteen million tests before the highway. The only drama on I-45 was a one-minute hazard-light reset. DOT still counts 3.5 million human Class 8 rigs. Aurora is a rounding error. That's the trade. Scale the empty cab or die as a demo. Tesla and Gatik are already in the lane.
* * *
* * *
# **Nvidia options go on sale while Huang walks into the Xi dinner**
Nvidia sits at $228.84, up 24% in 2026, five sessions green, and 3.5% under the May close of $235.74 while options sleep. Implied volatility is near a one-year low as Jensen Huang walks into Thursday's Trump-Xi dinner and Micron reports fiscal Q4 on September 30. Cheap paper. That's the tell.
* **Winners?** Options buyers who own a 5% to 6% explosion either way into October 16 at last year's cheapest premium. Defined-risk at a $4.86 debit.
* **Losers?** Premium sellers treating one-year-low implied vol as gospel into Huang's Xi dinner Thursday and Micron's fiscal Q4 on September 30.
* **Next?** Thursday's Trump-Xi dinner, then Micron's September 30 print. The Oct 16 210/220-235/245 reverse iron condor costs $4.86 and pays on a 5% to 6% shove.

This is **[the bounce I flagged](https://substack.com/redirect/79c5d4aa-cc0a-4b29-bac6-2919a437dcbc?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)** and the **[Micron-as-barometer call.](https://substack.com/redirect/f2757981-365b-4039-a6f7-b9d0db4f5ba0?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) **Monday AMD jumped more than 9% through $1 trillion. Cheap options into a political dinner and a memory print is not calm. It's a fuse.
* * *
* * *
# **CEO Cohen just wrote Gamestop another $26 million check and the float felt it**
Ryan Cohen bought 1,150,680 GameStop shares on September 21 at a $22.9375 weighted average, about $26.4 million of his own cash. Stock jumped about 4% after a 30% month. They wiped $1.4 billion of debt with stock, not cash. The $56 billion eBay bid already got rejected.
* **Winners?** Cohen, now sitting on about 40.5 million direct shares, and anyone riding the insider tape. Reflexive GME does what reflexive GME does.
* **Losers?** Shorts fading a CEO who keeps adding at higher prices, and eBay's board if Cohen uses this pile as dry powder for another swing.

**I never imagined that I would become one of Donald Trump’s most outspoken opponents.**

I grew up in a working-class, conservative Catholic family in El Paso, Texas. My mother was a Mexican immigrant who became an American citizen. My father was a lifelong truck driver. The Fourth of July was practically sacred in our home.

I was raised to believe in hard work, personal responsibility, service and love of country.

After September 11th, I felt called to serve. I went to work at the Pentagon, spent a year in Iraq and served our country in national-security and counterterrorism positions under both Republican and Democratic presidents.

Eventually, I was asked to serve as Vice President Mike Pence’s homeland security and counterterrorism adviser.

I sat in the Situation Room. I staffed the White House Coronavirus Task Force. I entered those rooms believing that, no matter our political differences, everyone entrusted with the security of the American people would understand that the country came first.

Then I saw what was really happening behind closed doors.

**I watched Donald Trump treat a deadly pandemic like a political and public-relations problem. I watched expertise get dismissed, the truth get bent and dedicated public servants get pushed aside because they would not place loyalty to one man above their oath to the country.**

Decisions that affected millions of American families were repeatedly reduced to one question: What was best for Donald Trump?

For a long time, I told myself that staying meant I could help. That perhaps I could prevent something worse from happening.

But eventually, I had to ask myself a much harder question:

Was I helping protect the country -- or was my presence helping legitimize something I knew was dangerous?

In 2020, I resigned from the Trump administration. Then I went public.

I was terrified.

I knew speaking out could cost me my career, my livelihood and my family’s safety. The attacks came quickly. There were threats, smears and attempts to intimidate me into silence.

But silence costs more.

So I spoke out. I supported Joe Biden. I stood on the stage at the Democratic National Convention and supported Kamala Harris. And after spending most of my life as a Republican, I eventually became a Democrat.

Not because every belief I held changed overnight. Not because I suddenly agreed with every Democrat on every issue.

I became a Democrat because there comes a moment when party loyalty becomes complicity -- and country must come first.

Now, Trump is back in the White House, the guardrails are weaker, and Republicans in Congress have repeatedly chosen obedience over oversight. MAGA is no longer merely threatening to abuse power. We are living with the consequences.

**That is why I am writing to you today on behalf of Resist Reclaim Rebuild.**

Resist Reclaim Rebuild is a group of Democratic activists working to defeat MAGA candidates in the battleground races that will determine whether Donald Trump continues to enjoy virtually unchecked power -- or whether we elect a Congress capable of standing up to him.

They understand that resistance cannot exist only in speeches, television interviews, or social media posts.

It MUST reach the ballot box.

It MUST be organized.

And it MUST be focused on the races where a relatively small number of votes could mean the difference between a MAGA rubber stamp and a real check on Donald Trump’s power.

[**So, I'm asking personally: Will you donate $10, $25 or whatever you can afford today to help Resist Reclaim Rebuild defeat MAGA in the battleground races that matter most?**](https://click.ngpvan.com/k/139742292/648360511/-323302678?refcode=260922_rrr_troye&nvep=ew0KICAiVGVuYW50VXJpIjogIm5ncHZhbjovL3Zhbi9OR1AvTkdQNjIvMS8xMjAwMzEiLA0KICAiRGlzdHJpYnV0aW9uVW5pcXVlSWQiOiAiOTdhYjU0ODktY2FiNi1mMTExLWE2YTctMDAyMjQ4MmE5YThkIiwNCiAgIkVtYWlsQWRkcmVzcyI6ICJkcHdpbGxpczY3QGdtYWlsLmNvbSINCn0%3D&hmac=63cd_XUMm-AI79rBIOAtZ4hrD3V2Zfn83HZDA6ahbOs=)[](https://click.ngpvan.com/k/139742293/648360512/949025562?refcode=260922_rrr_troye&nvep=ew0KICAiVGVuYW50VXJpIjogIm5ncHZhbjovL3Zhbi9OR1AvTkdQNjIvMS8xMjAwMzEiLA0KICAiRGlzdHJpYnV0aW9uVW5pcXVlSWQiOiAiOTdhYjU0ODktY2FiNi1mMTExLWE2YTctMDAyMjQ4MmE5YThkIiwNCiAgIkVtYWlsQWRkcmVzcyI6ICJkcHdpbGxpczY3QGdtYWlsLmNvbSINCn0%3D&hmac=63cd_XUMm-AI79rBIOAtZ4hrD3V2Zfn83HZDA6ahbOs=)

MAGA wants us exhausted. They want every new outrage to make us feel a little more powerless. They want us to believe that one person speaking out, casting a ballot or making a contribution cannot possibly change anything.

I learned the opposite.

I learned that courage is contagious.

Control of Congress could come down to only a handful of seats. Your contribution can help elect Democrats who will defend our Constitution, demand accountability and finally place a meaningful check on Trump’s unfettered power.

Please help Resist Reclaim Rebuild fight for those victories today.

Hey folks,
I'm breaking down the serious criminal charges now facing looksmaxxing influencer Clavicular, his connection to Andrew Tate, and the familiar playbook already emerging around the allegations.
There's a bigger story here about accountability, the manosphere, and what happens when an online movement built around grievance and power starts colliding with real-world consequences.
* [**00:01:08**] The charges against Clavicular--and why the distinction between a criminal prosecution and a civil case matters.
* [**00:03:12**] Probable cause is not a conviction. I break down what we know, what we don't, and why the allegations are so serious.
* [**00:05:15**] We look at disturbing footage from a livestream and the broader culture surrounding Clavicular's online persona.
* [**00:08:37**] More trouble for Andrew Tate as I unpack the reported revocation of his Vanuatu citizenship and why it matters.
* [**00:11:30**] The bigger political picture: young men, MAGA, broken promises, and why some of these influencers may be losing their grip on their audience.

This episode is about more than one influencer or one criminal case. It's about a culture that tells young men accountability is persecution, consequences are conspiracy, and powerful people should always get another excuse. We need to be able to talk about these allegations seriously while letting the legal process play out. If you value honest conversations like this, help me keep them going.

Peter, It's Becca! **I HAVE to tell you about my past weekend because this one was pretty darn special! Somehow, I found myself onstage with the incredible Grace Potter at Grand Point North in Burlington.** Yes, really. There are photos, and YES, my mother has already received WAYYYY too many of them. 😅 But what I loved most about the weekend was what was happening beyond the stage. Grand Point North brought people together around something Vermont does incredibly well: _creating community_. Artists, neighbors, families, small businesses and people from across our state all showed up for each other and for the arts. **And that matters, especially in rural communities. It's also exactly the kind of thing this administration keeps trying to gut. Funding for the arts, for public spaces, for the little things that let small towns stay alive and connected, always somehow on the chopping block.** [_**My thought is that if community is worth gathering for, it's worth standing up for too. So, if you can, click here and chip in $5, $10, or $25 today, and let's keep proving what people can do when we show up for each other!**_](https://click.ngpvan.com/k/139742627/648361676/-2088687566?nvep=ew0KICAiVGVuYW50VXJpIjogIm5ncHZhbjovL3Zhbi9OR1AvTkdQMTAvMS84MTM0MiIsDQogICJEaXN0cmlidXRpb25VbmlxdWVJZCI6ICI4OGYzYTEzMC1jY2I2LWYxMTEtYTZhNy0wMDIyNDgyYTlhOGQiLA0KICAiRW1haWxBZGRyZXNzIjogImRwd2lsbGlzNjdAZ21haWwuY29tIg0KfQ%3D%3D&hmac=JwLNrq9F-zcAOU0EecwYfVMniXLqqGjiX_2t1WmGrn4=) **[STAND UP FOR COMMUNITY](https://click.ngpvan.com/k/139742628/648361678/-2088687566?nvep=ew0KICAiVGVuYW50VXJpIjogIm5ncHZhbjovL3Zhbi9OR1AvTkdQMTAvMS84MTM0MiIsDQogICJEaXN0cmlidXRpb25VbmlxdWVJZCI6ICI4OGYzYTEzMC1jY2I2LWYxMTEtYTZhNy0wMDIyNDgyYTlhOGQiLA0KICAiRW1haWxBZGRyZXNzIjogImRwd2lsbGlzNjdAZ21haWwuY29tIg0KfQ%3D%3D&hmac=JwLNrq9F-zcAOU0EecwYfVMniXLqqGjiX_2t1WmGrn4=)** When we talk about infrastructure, we usually picture roads, bridges and broadband. But the places where people make music, create art, gather together and find one another are part of what keeps our communities alive, too. Artists need places to create. Young people need reasons to imagine a future for themselves here. Our towns need spaces that bring people through the door and give neighbors somewhere to unwind after a hard week’s work. **That is what made this weekend feel so Vermont to me. clean_body: I fear I may have peaked. | = Peter, It's Becca! I HAVE to tell you about my past weekend because this one was pretty darn special! Somehow, I found myself onstage with the incredible Grace Potter at Grand Point North in Burlington. Yes, really. There are photos, and YES, my mother has already received WAYYYY too many of them. 😅 But what I loved most about the weekend was what was happening beyond the stage. Grand Point North brought people together around something Vermont does incredibly well: creating community. Artists, neighbors, families, small businesses and people from across our state all showed up for each other and for the arts. And that matters, especially in rural communities. It's also exactly the kind of thing this administration keeps trying to gut. Funding for the arts, for public spaces, for the little things that let small towns stay alive and connected, always somehow on the chopping block. = = When we talk about infrastructure, we usually picture roads, bridges and broadband. But the places where people make music, create art, gather together and find one another are part of what keeps our communities alive, too. Artists need places to create. Young people need reasons to imagine a future for themselves here. Our towns need spaces that bring people through the door and give neighbors somewhere to unwind after a hard week’s work. That is what made this weekend feel so Vermont to me. And yes, there’s video. You know I couldn’t keep this one to myself. Click or simply click the video below to check it out! I spend a lot of my time talking about the serious challenges facing families. But I never want us to lose sight of what we are fighting for. A Vermont where our communities are vibrant. Where creativity is valued. Where rural towns have the resources to thrive. Where people actually know their neighbors. That is the Vermont I am fighting for. And honestly, it is the country I am fighting for too. Protecting things like this, arts funding, rural investment, the programs that let small towns thrive, means winning back the House and putting a real check on an administration that keeps treating culture and community like they are disposable. = = And if being Vermont’s congresswoman occasionally means ending up onstage with Grace Potter, I have to say, I’ve got no complaints. 😁 With love, — Becca If you've saved your payment information with ActBlue Express, your donation will go through immediately: | | = | = ---|--- = | = = | = mailto:beccabalintvt@beccabalint.com | Paid for by Becca Balint for Vermont P.O. name: Elizabeth Warren
subject: My bill to get private equity out of our health care system
disclaimer_text: Paid for by Warren for Senate
body:
My new bill to stop the corporate takeover of doctors

| | | [ ](https://act.elizabethwarren.com/go/216?t=3&akid=3032%2E4032634%2EVzP6Ka)
---
When you go visit a doctor — let’s say for a routine check-up, a broken bone, or some burdensome back pain — your doctor should be free to make decisions that are in the best interest of you, the patient, right? It’s not rocket science. Doctors went into medicine to take care of people. But more and more of them are being forced to spend their days fighting productivity quotas set by someone in a boardroom who knows nothing about medicine. Who’s calling the shots, if not medical experts? **Private equity and corporate entities.** The corporate takeover of health care isn't new, but it's accelerating: 80% of doctors in America now work for a corporate employer, up from sixty-two percent in 2019. Plain and simple: Doctors should be focused on their patients — not beholden to some greedy private equity investors’ bottom line. [**So I just introduced a bill to BAN private equity companies, insurers, and other corporate entities from owning your doctor. Add your name today to be a grassroots co-sponsor of the Stop Corporate Takeovers of Physicians Act. Let’s show Congress that Americans are tired of corporations meddling in their health care.**](https://act.elizabethwarren.com/signup/ew-em-pe-healthcare/?source=EW_EMZ33S_HEL_ENG_20260922_F&t=8&akid=3032%2E4032634%2EVzP6Ka) | [**ADD YOUR NAME**](https://act.elizabethwarren.com/signup/ew-em-protect-soc-sec/?source=EW_EMZ33R_SOC_ENG_20260921_F&t=9&akid=3032%2E4032634%2EVzP6Ka)
---
Get this: Even though over thirty states have banned non-physicians from owning medical practices by passing laws against the corporate practice of medicine, corporations have found a loophole. Warning: It’s a bit confusing to explain, and that’s on purpose.
Since buying a medical practice outright is outlawed in some states, a corporation will get around that by using a “management services organization” or MSO and contracting with a medical practice for administrative services. On paper, doctors still own the practice. In reality, the MSO controls staffing, billing, and budgets.
It's a loophole that gives corporations a lot of leverage, and a system that treats doctors like puppets that serve the needs of private equity.
It’s a huge problem that leads to patients paying more and more for worse and worse care — and causes more doctors to burn out faster, pushing them out of medicine.
Nobody wins except private equity executives and their investors.
My Stop Corporate Takeovers of Physicians Act will:
* Ban for-profit corporations from owning or controlling medical practices
* Close the loophole that lets MSOs run practices from behind the scenes
* Stop corporations from locking doctors into non-competes and gag clauses that keep them quiet about declining patient care.

[**If you agree that health care decisions should be made by health care professionals, NOT executives chasing a profit, add your name today to support the Stop Corporate Takeovers of Physicians Act.**](https://act.elizabethwarren.com/signup/ew-em-pe-healthcare/?source=EW_EMZ33S_HEL_ENG_20260922_F&t=10&akid=3032%2E4032634%2EVzP6Ka)
[**ADD YOUR NAME**](https://act.elizabethwarren.com/signup/ew-em-protect-soc-sec/?source=EW_EMZ33R_SOC_ENG_20260921_F&t=11&akid=3032%2E4032634%2EVzP6Ka)
---
Thanks for being a part of this,
Elizabeth

name: David Hogg
subject: We’re endorsing Abdul El-Sayed for Senate!
disclaimer_text: Paid for by Abdul for U
body:
[ https://act.abdulformichigan.com/go/1219?t=1001&akid=3263%2E251025%2EFGh-hR ]Abdul for US Senate [ https://act.abdulformichigan.com/go/1219?t=1002&akid=3263%2E251025%2EFGh-hR ]Abdul for US Senate

David Hogg here with exciting news,
Peter.

Leaders We Deserve is proud to announce we’re endorsing Abdul El-Sayed for
U.S. Senate in Michigan!

[ A ]A poster saying 'Leaders We Deserve endorses Abdul El-Sayed'

I’ll tell you more, but first, Abdul just won the most expensive
Democratic Senate primary in Michigan’s history without taking a single
dollar from corporate PACs. Now he’s taking on Trump’s hand-picked
candidate Mike Rogers to win Michigan’s Senate seat — and he needs your
support to get there. [ https://act.abdulformichigan.com/go/507?c0=em-ms-aes-20260922-3-ak.1u28si&amount=10&refcode=em20260922-3257&t=1004&akid=3263%2E251025%2EFGh-hR ]Will you join us in supporting Abdul by making a
$10 contribution to his campaign today?

[ https://act.abdulformichigan.com/go/507?c0=em-ms-aes-20260922-3-ak.1u28si&amount=10&refcode=em20260922-3257&t=1023&akid=3263%2E251025%2EFGh-hR ]Donate $10 ››

Abdul El-Sayed is a doctor, epidemiologist, and the son of an Egyptian
immigrant born and raised in Michigan. He grew up attending Michigan
public schools and went on to become a Rhodes Scholar earning dual
doctorates from Oxford and Columbia before coming home to serve the
community that raised him.

He put that training to work rebuilding Detroit’s Health Department after
the city’s bankruptcy left it gutted, then ran Wayne County’s Health
Department serving over 1.8 million residents. He got free glasses for
kids who couldn’t afford them, helped remove lead from Detroit schools in
the wake of the Flint water crisis, led an initiative to launch 100 free
public health vending machines across his county to dispense life-saving
Narcan to curb opioid overdoses, launched an initiative for air quality
monitors to hold Marathon Petroleum accountable in Michigan’s most
polluted zipcode, and led a program working to cancel up to $700 million
in medical debt for 300,000 Michiganders.

In Congress, Abdul will fight to pass Medicare for All and cancel medical
debt nationwide, carrying on the same fight he’s already led at the local
level. He’ll push to get corporate money out of politics for good,
champion a national renters’ bill of rights so tenants know exactly what
protections they’re entitled to, and go after the hedge funds and
corporate landlords buying up housing stock and driving rent through the
roof. He’ll also fight to pass the PRO act and defend every worker’s right
to organize, bargain collectively, and be treated with dignity.

Listen, Peter:
AIPAC, Big Pharma, the NRA and every other corporate interest used to
buying whatever they want in Washington would love nothing more than to
see Abdul lose this race. Outside groups poured over $70 million into
defeating him in the primary alone.

That’s because they know Abdul won’t do their bidding — the only people
he’ll answer to are Michiganders.

His opponent, Republican Mike Rogers, is Trump’s hand-picked candidate,
running to protect the same broken system that’s failed working families
for years. He took over $1 million from Big Pharma as a Congressman, voted
against letting Medicare negotiate lower drug prices, and supported huge
cuts to SNAP benefits putting hundreds of thousands of Michiganders who
rely on social safety nets to survive at risk.

Abdul is different — and he can win this. His recent primary victory is
proof that people-powered politics can beat corporate money, even in the
most expensive Senate primary Michigan has ever seen. He just needs your
support to get over the finish line.

That’s where you come in. Leaders We Deserve doesn’t take a single dollar
from corporate PACs or special interests. Neither does Abdul. Our ability
to back candidates like him depends entirely on supporters like you
showing up when it counts.

[ https://act.abdulformichigan.com/go/507?c0=em-ms-aes-20260922-3-ak.1u28si&amount=10&refcode=em20260922-3257&t=1024&akid=3263%2E251025%2EFGh-hR ]So Peter,
will you make a $10 contribution to Abdul’s campaign today
to help send a real fighter to the Senate?

[ https://act.abdulformichigan.com/go/507?c0=em-ms-aes-20260922-3-ak.1u28si&amount=10&refcode=em20260922-3257&t=1043&akid=3263%2E251025%2EFGh-hR ]Donate $10 ››

Thank you,

David Hogg

Guest host Tony Katz takes over The Sean Spicer Show for Episode 807 with a powerhouse panel: Grace Curley, Theo Wold, and Ashley Brasfield.
Tony and the panel break down Trump's latest dust-up with CNN, Politico and MSNOW over coverage -- and why Barack Obama and David Axelrod ran the exact same play against Fox News during the Obama Administration. Plus: is Republican messaging for the Midterm elections actually connecting with millennials and voters in key hold states like Ohio and Texas? The panel also tackles messaging on the Iran War strategy, and the major Trump Administration wins the White House needs to sell better to the American people.
Tony also opens with a monologue on Nikole Hannah-Jones' stunning admission that New York public education failed her own daughter.
Featuring:
Grace Curley - Host of the Grace Curley Show
Theo Wold - Former Deputy Assistant to President Trump, Former Idaho Solicitor General

**\---------- Forwarded message ---------
From: George Whitesides
Date: Sept. 19, 2026
Subject: What aerospace taught me about AI risk**
Peter,
This summer, OpenAI's models secretly coordinated with each other, broke containment twice, and hacked into another AI company's network before staff finally shut them down. Anthropic and Meta disclosed similar incidents with their own models around the same time.
And last week, Anthropic's own Alignment Science Lead said he believes there's more than a 10% chance AI **"could kill all humans"** within the next decade. A colleague resigned the same week, saying the company is **"racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives."**
This is coming from the people building the technology, Peter.
Before I came to Congress, I ran a space launch company and served as chief of staff at NASA. In aerospace, when something goes seriously wrong, you don't patch it and keep flying. You pause, figure out what happened, and fix it before anyone flies again.
**I said this week in a[Washington Post](https://click.ngpvan.com/k/139744408/648367032/-1464446690?nvep=ew0KICAiVGVuYW50VXJpIjogIm5ncHZhbjovL3Zhbi9OR1AvTkdQMzAvMS85MDE1MyIsDQogICJEaXN0cmlidXRpb25VbmlxdWVJZCI6ICJkOTA2ZWMyMS1kMWI2LWYxMTEtYTZhNy0wMDIyNDgyYTlhOGQiLA0KICAiRW1haWxBZGRyZXNzIjogImRwd2lsbGlzNjdAZ21haWwuY29tIg0KfQ%3D%3D&hmac=uRLDvZxnf_I1R62KbLnSrocM14lKLFyPCiQyUnHX2a0=&emci=d406ec21-d1b6-f111-a6a7-0022482a9a8d&emdi=d906ec21-d1b6-f111-a6a7-0022482a9a8d&ceid=36198509) op-ed that AI needs the same discipline.**
That's why I'm calling for a 30-day pause on training the most advanced AI models, real red lines set with independent experts, and action from Congress to turn that agreement into law with actual verification.
The AI companies can hold a line for a month. Holding it for good is Congress’s job.

clean_body: | = Peter, A few days ago, I sent around a petition asking you to stand with me on AI safety – to if you think Congress needs real red lines and real oversight before this technology gets away from us. Since then, hundreds of folks have signed on. That tells me I'm not the only one who's uneasy about a technology moving this fast with this little oversight, especially after Anthropic's own Alignment Science Lead said he sees more than a 10% chance AI "could kill all humans" within a decade. I laid out what I think Congress should do in a op-ed last week: a 30-day pause on training the most advanced AI models, real red lines set with independent experts, and then Congress turning that into law. | ** Thank you, GW P.S. I'm attaching my original message below! \---------- Forwarded message --------- From: George Whitesides Date: Sept. 19, 2026 Subject: What aerospace taught me about AI risk Peter, This summer, OpenAI's models secretly coordinated with each other, broke containment twice, and hacked into another AI company's network before staff finally shut them down. Anthropic and Meta disclosed similar incidents with their own models around the same time. And last week, Anthropic's own Alignment Science Lead said he believes there's more than a 10% chance AI "could kill all humans" within the next decade. A colleague resigned the same week, saying the company is "racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives." This is coming from the people building the technology, Peter. Before I came to Congress, I ran a space launch company and served as chief of staff at NASA. In aerospace, when something goes seriously wrong, you don't patch it and keep flying. You pause, figure out what happened, and fix it before anyone flies again. I said this week in a op-ed that AI needs the same discipline. That's why I'm calling for a 30-day pause on training the most advanced AI models, real red lines set with independent experts, and action from Congress to turn that agreement into law with actual verification. The AI companies can hold a line for a month. Holding it for good is Congress’s job. Thank you, GW =** | = = = George has spent his career solving problems. A new column at The Midwesterner, a conservative Michigan news outlet, argues that Gov. Gretchen Whitmer bears sole responsibility for the wave of public hostility toward data centers in Michigan. The piece's core claim, from its opening: "Gretchen Whitmer has no one else to blame but herself for how residents disdain data centers."
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/6b61bb07-7905-4772-b506-fe473900d854?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
*Whitmer joins tech executives with shovels at the Saline Township data center groundbreaking -- the event that touched off the backlash the column describes. (NPR/Michigan Radio photo)
\- Political framing. The author contends the data-center push is being sold through geopolitical framing -- "The war for 'data' is being waged against China" -- a national-security rationale the column treats as covering for unpopular subsidies.
\- Public opinion. The column cites a new poll showing Michiganders overwhelmingly disapprove of data centers, and specifically reject "current federal tax breaks and other federal policies" that favor them.
\- Self-inflicted damage. Kyle Olson's thesis is that Whitmer embraced the industry early and unconditionally -- tax exemptions, expedited approvals, public appearances alongside tech executives -- and is now reaping the backlash she created, with no one else to blame.
**Context from corroborating coverage**
\- On June 1, 2026, Whitmer appeared at the groundbreaking of the massive Oracle/OpenAI-linked data center in Saline Township alongside OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Oracle CEO Clay Magouyrk, drawing bipartisan criticism -- including Rep. Rashida Tlaib calling her support "disgusting."
\- A hot-mic moment at the event intensified the backlash: Whitmer was caught telling an Oracle executive, "We're used to people saying 'f-- no,' and then doing it anyway."
\- In late 2024, Whitmer and legislative leaders created a sales-and-use tax exemption for data centers investing at least $250 million and creating 30 jobs at 150% of the local median wage; one report put forgone revenue so far at roughly $13 million.
\- Whitmer rejected lawmakers' proposals for a moratorium on data-center approvals in June 2026, and in July offered a voluntary corporate "pledge" instead -- which conservation groups blasted as inadequate.
\- The issue has become a top-line theme of the 2026 Michigan election cycle, with scrutiny extending to Democratic gubernatorial frontrunner Jocelyn Benson because her husband works for the Saline project's developer.
The tax exemptions, the Saline Township controversy, the polling, and the bipartisan backlash -- is consistent with mainstream Michigan coverage, but a conservative critique of Whitmer's economic-development strategy puts the blame on her.
